description: coFlipper command catalog, on two layers. 'device' = CFP commands sent over the serial port to the Flipper ('cfp <id> <name> [arguments]', see /PROTOCOL.md), executed directly by the hardware. Some device commands (category 'wifi' and 'ble', marked 'requires': 'wifi_dev_board') are served not by the Flipper itself but by an ESP32 Wi-Fi dev board flashed with Marauder firmware and attached to the Flipper's GPIO/UART header; the Flipper's CFP application forwards them to the board. 'agent' = high-level operations, executed on the desktop, which combine one or more device commands with LLM (Gemini) reasoning - this is the original part of the project, not the device commands taken individually, which replicate functions already present in the Flipper Zero / Marauder firmware. Each device command also carries an 'impact' field ('passive' = only listens/reads, 'offensive' = transmits and disrupts other devices, needs the user's authorization) to help the agent reason about consequences. Commands with 'agent_visible': false are for internal use and are not exposed to the model as callable tools.
_note_subghz_listen: The Sub-GHz 'listen' feature spans both layers: subghz.read is the device primitive (decode one packet), agent.listen loops it over a time window through the listener subagent to harvest the LIST of distinct devices on a frequency and save each as a descriptively named .sub in apps_assets, and agent.replay_subghz re-emits a saved capture by its descriptive name (offensive, gated on authorization).

commands.name: ping
commands.description: Checks whether the CFP server on the Flipper responds.
commands.returns: pong

commands.name: info
commands.description: The name/model of the connected Flipper device.
commands.returns: the hardware model name

commands.name: device.battery
commands.description: The current battery level and whether it is charging.
commands.returns: battery percentage, charging state

commands.name: device.storage.list
commands.description: Lists the files saved on the SD card in a given folder (saved IR/Sub-GHz signals, saved NFC cards, etc.).

args.name: path
args.description: path on the SD card, e.g. /ext/subghz

commands.returns: a list of file names

commands.name: exit
commands.description: Closes the CFP application on the Flipper, remotely. Needed during development: reinstalling the application requires the previous instance to be closed, and without this command the Back button would have to be pressed physically on every iteration.
commands.returns: close confirmation

commands.name: subghz.rssi
commands.description: Measures the signal level (RSSI, in dBm) on a given frequency, listening for approximately 100 ms. Values close to -50 dBm indicate a strong signal, those below -90 dBm generally indicate only background noise. It does not decode the signal, only quantifies its presence.

args.name: frequency
args.description: frequency in Hz, e.g. 433920000

commands.returns: the frequency actually synthesized by the radio (Hz) and the peak RSSI value (dBm)

commands.name: subghz.scan
commands.description: Scans a list of known frequencies and reports on which of them activity is detected (RSSI above a threshold).

args.name: duration_ms
args.description: scan duration, 3000 by default

commands.returns: a list of frequencies with a detected signal

commands.name: subghz.read
commands.description: Listens on ONE frequency and decodes the NEXT single Sub-GHz packet that arrives, identifying its protocol - the low-level primitive behind Sub-GHz capture. It tunes the CC1101 transceiver to the given frequency, waits up to timeout_ms for a transmission, and if one is decoded returns its protocol name (e.g. Princeton, CAME, KeeLoq, Nice_FloR_S), the key/code carried, and the bit-length, together with the frequency the radio actually synthesised and the signal's RSSI. It captures AT MOST ONE signal per call: if the air is busy it returns the first packet it decodes and stops, and if nothing arrives within the timeout it returns 'no_signal'. This is passive - it only receives, it transmits nothing. To harvest EVERYTHING transmitting on a shared frequency (several unrelated devices at once), do not call this once; call agent.listen, which loops over subghz.read across a time window and returns the whole list of distinct devices. Successive calls on the same frequency return successive packets, so a device that keeps repeating is not re-reported endlessly.

args.name: frequency
args.description: frequency in Hz, must fall in a CC1101 band (300-348, 387-464 or 779-928 MHz), e.g. 433920000

args.name: timeout_ms
args.description: how long it waits for a packet before giving up, 5000 by default

commands.returns: either 'signal' followed by protocol, key, bit-length, the frequency actually synthesised (Hz) and RSSI (dBm); or 'no_signal' if nothing was decoded within the timeout

commands.name: subghz.replay
commands.description: Retransmits a Sub-GHz signal from a saved .sub file: it reads the file's frequency and code and keys the CC1101 transceiver to re-emit that exact signal. THIS TRANSMITS on the radio and can actuate the real device the signal belongs to (open a gate, trigger a relay), so it is only for testing one's own devices, never someone else's. It takes a raw filesystem path; prefer the agent-layer agent.replay_subghz, which lets the user name a capture descriptively ('the doorbell one') and resolves it to the right file, instead of calling this with a path directly. Requires the user's explicit authorization first (see agent.confirm_authorized_action).

args.name: file
args.description: absolute path to the saved .sub file to transmit

commands.returns: transmission confirmation, echoing back the file that was replayed

commands.name: ir.read
commands.description: Waits for and decodes the next IR signal received (e.g. a button press on a remote pointed at the Flipper).

args.name: timeout_ms
args.description: how long it waits for a signal, 5000 by default

commands.returns: the decoded protocol, address, and command

commands.name: ir.learn
commands.description: Learns a new IR signal (from a physical remote) and saves it under a given name, for later reuse.

args.name: name
args.description: the name to save the signal under, e.g. tv_power

commands.returns: save confirmation

commands.name: ir.send
commands.description: Retransmits a previously saved IR signal (universal remote functionality).

args.name: name
args.description: the name of the saved signal, e.g. tv_power

commands.returns: transmission confirmation

commands.name: ir.queue
commands.description: Adds one IR code to the list pending transmission. Queueing is separate from transmitting because a CFP v1 frame cannot carry a whole code list: one frame queues one code.

args.name: protocol
args.description: IR protocol name, e.g. NEC, Samsung32, SIRC, RC5

args.name: address
args.description: device address, hexadecimal, e.g. 0x07

args.name: command
args.description: command byte, hexadecimal, e.g. 0x02

commands.returns: how many codes are queued

commands.name: ir.bruteforce
commands.description: Starts transmitting the queued IR codes, one every 250 ms, showing a progress bar on the Flipper's screen. Returns as soon as the run has started, not when it finishes: the run lasts several seconds, far longer than the client's read timeout. The user stops it by pressing the middle (OK) button on the device when the appliance reacts.

args.name: label
args.description: what is being bruteforced, shown on the device screen; no spaces

commands.returns: start confirmation and the number of queued codes

commands.name: ir.status
commands.description: How far the bruteforce has got: state (running/stopped/idle), how many codes have been sent, and how many were queued. 'stopped' means the user pressed OK on the device, i.e. the appliance responded to the code just sent.
commands.returns: state, codes sent, codes queued

commands.name: ir.reset
commands.description: Clears the queued IR codes, so the next run starts from a clean slate.
commands.returns: clear confirmation

commands.name: nfc.read
commands.description: Waits for an NFC tag/card brought close to the Flipper and returns its UID and type.

args.name: timeout_ms
args.description: how long it waits for a card, 5000 by default

commands.returns: UID, card type (Mifare, NTAG, etc.)

commands.name: nfc.watch
commands.description: Monitors, over a period of time, all NFC tags/cards that come within range of the module.

args.name: duration_ms
args.description: monitoring duration in milliseconds

commands.returns: a list of detected card UIDs/types, in chronological order, with timestamps

commands.name: nfc.emulate
commands.description: Emulates a previously saved NFC card (the Flipper behaves like that card towards a reader).

args.name: name
args.description: the name of the saved card

commands.returns: emulation start confirmation

commands.name: rfid.read
commands.description: Reads a low-frequency RFID card (125 kHz) brought close to the Flipper.

args.name: timeout_ms
args.description: how long it waits for a card, 5000 by default

commands.returns: card ID, protocol (EM4100, HID, etc.)

commands.name: wifi.board_info
commands.description: Reports the presence and firmware of the Wi-Fi dev board - an ESP32 flashed with Marauder firmware, attached to the Flipper's GPIO/UART header - together with the Marauder version and hardware model. Call this first whenever the user asks anything about Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, to confirm the board is attached before attempting any wifi.* or ble.* operation. If no board is present it returns the error 'wifi_board_not_connected'.
commands.returns: board presence, Marauder firmware version, hardware model

commands.name: wifi.set_channel
commands.description: Locks the Wi-Fi radio to a specific 2.4 GHz channel (1-14). Scans and sniffs only see traffic on the current channel, so set the channel of a target access point (from wifi.list_ap) before sniffing its clients or capturing its handshake. Rejects channels outside 1-14 with 'invalid_channel'.

args.name: channel
args.description: 2.4 GHz channel, 1 to 14

commands.returns: the channel the radio is now tuned to

commands.name: wifi.scan_ap
commands.description: Scans the surrounding 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi for access points (routers/hotspots) and stores what it finds in the board's access-point list. Passive: it only listens to the beacons networks already broadcast, it does not transmit. Run this before wifi.list_ap, and before selecting a target for any attack. A scan runs for a short window and then returns how many access points were captured.

args.name: duration_ms
args.description: how long to listen, 8000 by default

commands.returns: how many access points were captured

commands.name: wifi.scan_station
commands.description: Scans for client stations (phones, laptops, IoT devices) associated with the access points already captured, and stores them in the station list. Passive listening only. Run wifi.scan_ap first so there are access points to attribute the clients to. A station is what you target for a client-specific deauthentication.

args.name: duration_ms
args.description: how long to listen, 8000 by default

commands.returns: how many client stations were captured

commands.name: wifi.list_ap
commands.description: Lists the access points captured by the last wifi.scan_ap. Each entry is one token 'index;SSID;BSSID;channel;rssi;encryption' (fields separated by semicolons, no spaces). The index is the handle used by wifi.select_ap to choose a target. Use this to show the user which networks are in range so they can pick one, instead of acting on all of them blindly.
commands.returns: one token per access point: index, SSID, BSSID, channel, RSSI, encryption

commands.name: wifi.list_station
commands.description: Lists the client stations captured by the last wifi.scan_station. Each entry is one token 'index;MAC;ap_index;rssi'. The index is the handle used by wifi.select_station.
commands.returns: one token per station: index, MAC, associated access-point index, RSSI

commands.name: wifi.select_ap
commands.description: Marks one or more access points from the list as the current target for a subsequent attack (wifi.attack_deauth, wifi.attack_beacon_clone). The selector is an index ('2'), a range ('0-3'), a comma list ('0,4,5') or 'all'. Selecting a target does nothing on its own; it only decides what the next attack will act on. Prefer selecting the specific network the user named over 'all'.

args.name: targets
args.description: index, range like 0-3, comma list like 0,4,5, or the word all

commands.returns: how many access points are now selected

commands.name: wifi.select_station
commands.description: Marks one or more client stations from the list as the current target, for a client-specific deauthentication. Same selector syntax as wifi.select_ap.

args.name: targets
args.description: index, range, comma list, or the word all

commands.returns: how many stations are now selected

commands.name: wifi.clear_targets
commands.description: Clears the captured access-point and station lists and any current selection, so the next scan starts from a clean slate.
commands.returns: confirmation that the lists were cleared

commands.name: wifi.sniff_beacon
commands.description: Captures raw beacon frames (the periodic advertisements access points broadcast). Passive monitoring, useful for surveying every network announcing itself, including hidden or spoofed ones. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that beacon sniffing has started

commands.name: wifi.sniff_probe
commands.description: Captures probe-request frames: the messages client devices send out looking for known networks. Passive. It reveals which networks nearby phones/laptops have connected to before, and is the reconnaissance step behind a karma-style attack. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that probe sniffing has started

commands.name: wifi.sniff_deauth
commands.description: Listens for deauthentication frames in the air - a defensive tool: it detects whether someone else is running a deauth attack nearby. Passive, transmits nothing. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that deauth-detection sniffing has started

commands.name: wifi.sniff_pmkid
commands.description: Captures WPA/WPA2 handshake material (PMKID and EAPOL frames) from the selected or current-channel access point, and saves it for offline analysis. Passive capture of authentication traffic; often combined with a brief deauth of a client to force it to reconnect and produce a fresh handshake. Only capture handshakes for a network the user owns or is authorized to test. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that handshake capture has started, and how many handshakes were seen

commands.name: wifi.sniff_pwnagotchi
commands.description: Detects nearby Pwnagotchi units by their characteristic beacon advertisements. Passive. A curiosity/recon tool. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that Pwnagotchi detection has started

commands.name: wifi.sniff_raw
commands.description: Captures raw 802.11 packets on the current channel for later inspection or saving to a pcap. Passive. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that raw capture has started

commands.name: wifi.sniff_esp
commands.description: Detects other ESP32/ESP8266 devices transmitting nearby. Passive recon. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that ESP detection has started

commands.name: wifi.attack_deauth
commands.description: Sends 802.11 deauthentication frames against the currently selected access point(s) (wifi.select_ap) or station(s) (wifi.select_station), forcing the associated clients to disconnect. THIS IS AN ACTIVE ATTACK that disrupts a real network. Send it ONLY after the user has explicitly confirmed they own the target network or have authorization to test it, and only against a specific selected target - never a broad selection - unless the user asked for exactly that. Requires a selection first; returns 'no_target_selected' otherwise. Keeps transmitting until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that the deauth attack has started, and against how many targets

commands.name: wifi.attack_deauth_all
commands.description: Deauthenticates EVERY access point currently in range, indiscriminately. This is a broad, disruptive attack that knocks nearby networks offline; it is almost never what a legitimate test needs. Strongly prefer wifi.attack_deauth against one selected target. Use only when the user explicitly asks to affect all networks AND confirms authorization for the whole environment (for example an isolated lab). Keeps transmitting until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that the broad deauth has started, and against how many access points

commands.name: wifi.attack_beacon_random
commands.description: Floods the air with beacon frames advertising randomly named fake networks, so a swarm of bogus SSIDs appears in every device's Wi-Fi list. Active transmission that clutters the spectrum; confirm the user is authorized to transmit in this environment before starting. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.

args.name: count
args.description: how many fake SSIDs to broadcast, 20 by default

commands.returns: confirmation that beacon spam has started

commands.name: wifi.attack_beacon_list
commands.description: Broadcasts beacon frames for every SSID in the user-defined list (built with wifi.ssid_add / wifi.ssid_generate), making those exact network names appear nearby. Active transmission; confirm authorization first. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that list-based beacon spam has started

commands.name: wifi.attack_beacon_clone
commands.description: Broadcasts beacons impersonating the SSID of the currently selected access point (wifi.select_ap), creating a look-alike of that specific network - the beacon half of an evil-twin. Active transmission that impersonates someone's network; only against a network the user owns or is authorized to test, after explicit confirmation. Requires a selection; returns 'no_target_selected' otherwise. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that the clone beacon has started

commands.name: wifi.attack_probe_flood
commands.description: Floods the channel with probe-request frames, which can stress access points that log or respond to them. Active transmission; confirm authorization first. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that the probe flood has started

commands.name: wifi.attack_rickroll
commands.description: A harmless-prank variant of beacon spam: broadcasts fake networks whose SSIDs spell out the lyrics of a well-known song. Still an active transmission that adds bogus networks to everyone's Wi-Fi list, so confirm the user is authorized to transmit here. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that the rickroll beacon spam has started

commands.name: wifi.evil_portal
commands.description: Stands up a fake open access point with a captive-portal login page (an evil twin), so devices that connect are shown a page that can harvest whatever the page asks for. This is a phishing-capable attack and must only be used on the user's own network or in an explicitly authorized engagement, with clear confirmation. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.

args.name: ssid
args.description: the network name to advertise; if omitted, the selected AP's SSID is cloned

commands.returns: confirmation that the evil portal has started

commands.name: wifi.karma
commands.description: Answers the probe requests captured from nearby devices by impersonating whatever network name each device is looking for, luring it to connect. Active impersonation attack; authorized testing only, with explicit confirmation. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that the karma attack has started

commands.name: wifi.wardrive
commands.description: Continuously logs every access point seen together with the GPS position it was seen at (requires a GPS module on the board), building a wardriving map on the SD card. Passive: it only records the beacons networks already broadcast. Runs until stopped with wifi.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that wardriving has started

commands.name: wifi.ssid_add
commands.description: Adds one SSID (network name) to the user-defined SSID list used by wifi.attack_beacon_list. Building the list does nothing on the air by itself. The name cannot contain spaces (CFP v1 limitation).

args.name: ssid
args.description: the network name to add, without spaces

commands.returns: confirmation, and the new size of the list

commands.name: wifi.ssid_generate
commands.description: Fills the user-defined SSID list with a number of randomly generated network names, as raw material for wifi.attack_beacon_list. Does nothing on the air by itself.

args.name: count
args.description: how many random SSIDs to generate

commands.returns: confirmation, and the new size of the list

commands.name: wifi.ssid_list
commands.description: Lists the SSIDs currently in the user-defined list, one token per name.
commands.returns: the SSIDs in the list

commands.name: wifi.gps_data
commands.description: Reads the current fix from a GPS module attached to the board (used by wifi.wardrive): latitude, longitude, satellite count. Returns a no-fix status if no GPS module is present or no satellites are locked. Passive.
commands.returns: latitude, longitude, satellites in view, or a no-fix status

commands.name: wifi.save_pcap
commands.description: Writes the packets captured so far (from any sniff.* operation) to a .pcap file on the Flipper's SD card, for later analysis on a computer.
commands.returns: the path of the saved capture file

commands.name: wifi.stop
commands.description: Stops whatever Wi-Fi operation is currently running (a scan, a sniff, or an attack). Marauder operations run continuously until stopped, so send this as soon as the user's goal is met, and always before starting a different one. Also stops any ongoing attack immediately.
commands.returns: confirmation that the current operation stopped

commands.name: ble.scan
commands.description: Scans for Bluetooth Low Energy devices advertising nearby and stores them in the BLE device list. Passive listening. Run before ble.list. The board's Marauder firmware handles BLE in addition to Wi-Fi.

args.name: duration_ms
args.description: how long to listen, 8000 by default

commands.returns: how many BLE devices were captured

commands.name: ble.list
commands.description: Lists the BLE devices captured by the last ble.scan. Each entry is one token 'index;MAC;name;rssi'.
commands.returns: one token per device: index, MAC, advertised name, RSSI

commands.name: ble.sniff_airtag
commands.description: Scans specifically for Apple AirTags and other Find My / BLE trackers advertising nearby - useful for detecting whether an unknown tracker is following someone. Passive. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that AirTag/tracker detection has started, and how many were seen

commands.name: ble.spam_apple
commands.description: Broadcasts fake Apple proximity-pairing BLE advertisements (the 'sour apple' effect), making nearby iPhones/iPads show a stream of spurious pairing pop-ups. Active transmission that harasses nearby devices; confirm the user is authorized to transmit in this environment before starting. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that Apple BLE spam has started

commands.name: ble.spam_android
commands.description: Broadcasts fake Google/Android Fast Pair BLE advertisements, making nearby Android phones show spurious pairing notifications. Active transmission; confirm authorization first. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that Android BLE spam has started

commands.name: ble.spam_samsung
commands.description: Broadcasts fake Samsung Galaxy buds/watch BLE advertisements, triggering spurious pairing pop-ups on nearby Samsung devices. Active transmission; confirm authorization first. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that Samsung BLE spam has started

commands.name: ble.spam_windows
commands.description: Broadcasts fake Microsoft Swift Pair BLE advertisements, triggering spurious pairing notifications on nearby Windows machines. Active transmission; confirm authorization first. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that Windows BLE spam has started

commands.name: ble.spam_all
commands.description: Broadcasts BLE pairing advertisements for all supported vendors at once (Apple, Android, Samsung, Windows) - the most disruptive BLE-spam mode, affecting every nearby phone and laptop. Active, broad harassment; use only with explicit authorization for the whole environment. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that all-vendor BLE spam has started

commands.name: ble.spam_airtag
commands.description: Broadcasts many fake Apple Find My (AirTag) advertisements at once, so nearby Apple devices see a cloud of bogus trackers. Active transmission; confirm authorization first. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that AirTag spoofing has started

commands.name: ble.detect_flipper
commands.description: Detects other Flipper Zero devices advertising over BLE nearby. Passive recon. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that Flipper detection has started, and how many were seen

commands.name: ble.wardrive
commands.description: Continuously logs every BLE device seen together with its GPS position (requires a GPS module), building a Bluetooth wardriving map on the SD card. Passive. Runs until stopped with ble.stop.
commands.returns: confirmation that BLE wardriving has started

commands.name: ble.stop
commands.description: Stops whatever BLE operation is currently running (a scan, a tracker sniff, or a spam). Send it as soon as the user's goal is met, and before starting a different BLE operation.
commands.returns: confirmation that the current BLE operation stopped

commands.name: marauder.reboot
commands.description: Reboots the ESP32 Wi-Fi board running Marauder. Useful when the board has become unresponsive or is stuck in a previous operation that wifi.stop did not clear.
commands.returns: confirmation that the board is rebooting

commands.name: agent.check_frequency_activity
commands.description: Delegates to the scanner subagent the monitoring of a frequency over several successive readings, in order to establish whether anything is actually transmitting on it. Use this instead of subghz.rssi whenever the question is about activity rather than about one instantaneous value: a single reading cannot distinguish an empty frequency from a transmitter that happens to be silent at that instant. It takes longer, since it performs several measurements, and it returns an interpreted conclusion together with all the readings behind it.
commands.task: Establish whether there is real radio activity on the requested frequency. Take several readings of the signal level, spaced out, and judge by the whole set: the maximum reached, how much the values vary, and whether anything stands out above the background noise. If no frequency was given, use the common ISM frequencies (433.92 MHz and 868.35 MHz).

args.name: frequency
args.description: the frequency of interest, in Hz; if absent, the common ISM frequencies are used

args.name: readings
args.description: how many successive readings to take, 4 by default

commands.returns: an interpreted conclusion about the activity, plus the raw readings it rests on

commands.name: agent.listen
commands.description: Delegates to the listener subagent the harvesting of a Sub-GHz frequency over a window of time: instead of capturing one packet, it listens repeatedly across the whole duration and returns the LIST of DISTINCT devices heard on that frequency, each identified and saved. This is the command for the situation where several unrelated things share one frequency - the classic 433.92 MHz case where an electric relay, a doorbell remote, a car fob and a weather sensor are all transmitting at once. A single subghz.read would catch only whichever fired first; agent.listen loops over subghz.read for the whole window, deduplicates the captures by protocol and key, guesses what each device is from its protocol and frequency, and writes each distinct signal to disk in the apps_assets folder as a .sub file with a DESCRIPTIVE name (band + protocol + the guess, e.g. '433MHz_Princeton_wireless_doorbell_remote_4e7b90.sub') so it can be found again by a later search and replayed with agent.replay_subghz. Use this - not subghz.read - whenever the user wants to know 'what is transmitting on this frequency' or to record a device's signal. The subagent is PASSIVE: it only receives and writes files, it transmits nothing, so it can never actuate a device on its own. It takes longer than a single read and costs several requests, since it performs many captures. If no frequency is given it defaults to 433.92 MHz, the busiest ISM band.
commands.task: Listen on the given frequency for the given number of seconds and harvest every DISTINCT Sub-GHz signal transmitting on it. Optionally confirm activity with one subghz.rssi reading first; then call subghz.read in a loop across the window, stopping early if two consecutive reads return no_signal. Deduplicate captures by protocol AND key, so a repeating device counts once. For each distinct signal, guess what the source device is from its protocol and frequency (a doorbell, a relay, a car fob, a sensor), stating it is a guess. Save each distinct signal with save_subghz, passing a specific plain-English guess so the saved file is descriptively named and findable. If no frequency was given, use 433.92 MHz. Report the harvested list: for each device, its protocol, key, RSSI, your guess, and the name it was saved under.

args.name: frequency
args.description: the frequency to listen on, in Hz, e.g. 433920000; defaults to 433.92 MHz if omitted

args.name: time
args.description: how long to listen, in seconds; the subagent turns this into a number of successive reads. 20 by default

commands.returns: the list of distinct Sub-GHz devices harvested from the frequency, each with its protocol, key, RSSI, a guess at the source, and the descriptive name it was saved under in apps_assets; plus the raw captures behind it

commands.name: agent.watch_subghz
commands.description: Delegates to the watcher subagent the WAITING for a Sub-GHz signal that has not been sent yet, over a bounded window, and reports the FIRST real transmission it catches. This is the command for the situation where the user announces that a signal is about to be played or triggered - 'a Sub-GHz signal is going to be played shortly, listen for it', 'I'm about to press the fob, watch 433.92', 'catch the next signal on this frequency'. The watcher polls subghz.read in a loop across the window and stops the instant a signal is decoded, reporting its protocol, key, bit-length and RSSI plus a guess at the source device; if the whole window passes with nothing on the air, it reports plainly that nothing was heard rather than inventing a signal. This differs from the other Sub-GHz commands by intent: subghz.rssi is one instantaneous level; agent.check_frequency_activity decides whether anything is transmitting NOW; agent.listen harvests the LIST of everything already transmitting across a full window; agent.watch_subghz WAITS for a single upcoming signal and reacts to it. The watcher is PASSIVE: it only receives, it transmits nothing. It takes up to the window's length and costs several requests. If no frequency is given it defaults to 433.92 MHz; if no time is given it watches for 15 seconds.
commands.task: Wait on the given frequency for the given number of seconds and report the FIRST Sub-GHz signal that arrives. Optionally take one subghz.rssi reading to note the resting background level; then call subghz.read in a loop across the window. A no_signal result is the expected case while waiting - keep reading. The instant a read returns a 'signal' result, STOP and report it: its protocol, key, bit-length and RSSI exactly as returned, plus a plain-English guess at what the device is (a doorbell, a car fob, a relay, a sensor), stated as a guess, and say clearly the signal WAS heard. If the whole window passes with only no_signal, report plainly that nothing was heard in the window - do not invent a signal, and do not claim the frequency is dead. If no frequency was given, use 433.92 MHz; if no time was given, watch for 15 seconds.

args.name: frequency
args.description: the frequency to watch, in Hz, e.g. 433920000; defaults to 433.92 MHz if omitted

args.name: time
args.description: how long to wait for the signal, in seconds; the subagent turns this into a number of successive reads. 15 by default

commands.returns: the first Sub-GHz signal caught in the window - its protocol, key, bit-length, RSSI and a guess at the source device - or a plain statement that nothing was heard in the window; plus the raw reads behind it

commands.name: agent.run_script
commands.description: Writes and runs a SHORT, TEMPORARY Python script for one situation that no single catalog command covers - custom logic combining several device operations: polling a frequency until a value settles or a signal appears, chaining a handful of reads under a condition, timing a sequence, retrying until something happens, or computing a result across several readings. Use this whenever you judge that a small piece of custom logic is the right tool and no dedicated command (subghz.rssi, agent.listen, agent.watch_subghz, agent.check_frequency_activity, the IR tools) already does the job; prefer a dedicated command when one fits, and reach for a script only for the case it does not. The script runs in a locked-down sandbox: a separate Python process with a hard time limit, given ONLY a small set of harmless stdlib modules (time, math, json, random, statistics) and one object, `flipper`, whose single method flipper.request(command, *args) sends a device command and returns the usual {'status','data'} result dict. The script has NO access to the filesystem, the network, os or subprocess - it can compute and it can talk to the Flipper, nothing else. Write to stdout with print(): whatever the script prints is returned to you as its output, alongside the list of every device command it actually ran (check your conclusions against those, never against the printed text alone). A device command that TRANSMITS (subghz.replay, ir.send, nfc.emulate, offensive wifi/ble) is just as offensive when a script sends it as when you call it directly: run the authorization gate (agent.confirm_authorized_action) BEFORE running any script that transmits, and keep scripts passive unless the user has authorized otherwise. The script cannot run forever: it is killed at its time limit and reported as timed out, so keep the logic bounded.

args.name: purpose
args.description: one short line on what this script is for, e.g. 'poll 433.92 MHz until a signal is decoded or 15 s pass'

args.name: code
args.description: the Python source to run. Talk to the device with flipper.request('subghz.read', 433920000) and read result['status']/result['data']; print() what you want returned. Only time, math, json, random and statistics may be imported.

args.name: timeout
args.description: wall-clock limit in seconds before the script is killed; 20 by default, 60 at most

commands.returns: the script's printed output, the list of device commands it ran with their real results, and whether it was stopped for exceeding its time limit

commands.name: agent.replay_subghz
commands.description: Retransmits a Sub-GHz signal previously harvested and saved by agent.listen, named the way the user refers to it ('replay the doorbell one', 'send the relay signal') rather than by file path. It looks the capture up in the apps_assets folder by a substring of its descriptive name, resolves it to the exact .sub file, and sends the device-layer subghz.replay to re-emit it. If the name matches no capture, or matches several, it says so and lists the candidates instead of guessing - replaying the wrong signal is exactly the mistake to avoid. THIS IS AN OFFENSIVE, TRANSMITTING action: it keys the radio and can actuate the real device the signal belongs to (open a gate, ring a doorbell, trip a relay). Send it ONLY after the user has explicitly confirmed they own the device or are authorized to test it (see agent.confirm_authorized_action). Use agent.listen first to capture and save the signal; use list_subghz-style listing (or just tell the user) to see what is available to replay.

args.name: name
args.description: the capture to replay, as a substring of its descriptive name, e.g. 'doorbell' or 'relay' or the full saved name

commands.returns: confirmation of which saved capture was replayed and from which file, or an error listing the available captures if the name was ambiguous or unknown

commands.name: agent.research_session_log
commands.description: Delegates to the analyst subagent the researching of the session log: every command executed on the device so far, with its arguments, results and errors. Use this for questions about what has already been done ('what have we measured so far?', 'which commands failed?', 'was this frequency checked before?'). The analyst has no access to the device, so it can only answer from the recorded history, never with a new measurement.
commands.task: Research the session log below and answer the question asked. Rely exclusively on what the log contains, and state explicitly what it does not contain but would be needed for a complete answer.

args.name: question
args.description: what should be established from the session history

commands.returns: an answer drawn from the session log, with the gaps in it stated explicitly

commands.name: agent.wifi_recon
commands.description: Delegates to the wifi_recon subagent a full passive survey of the Wi-Fi (and optionally BLE) environment: it confirms the board, scans for access points and their clients, reads the lists, and reports back an interpreted picture - how many networks, which are open vs encrypted, which are busiest, and which stand out as plausible targets for the user's stated goal. Use this instead of calling the individual scan/list commands yourself whenever the user asks an open question about 'what is around' or 'find the network X', since it takes several successive scans and interprets the whole. The subagent is passive by design: it has NO attack tools and can only listen, so it can never start a deauth or spam on its own - any offensive action stays your decision, taken with the user, afterwards.
commands.task: Survey the Wi-Fi environment and report an interpreted picture of it. Confirm the Wi-Fi board is present, scan for access points and their client stations, read the lists, and summarise: how many networks, their encryption, which channels are busy, which clients are active, and - in light of what the main agent asked for - which access points or stations are the plausible targets. Do not attack anything; you have no tools to do so. If a specific network was named, say whether it was found and give its index, channel and encryption.

args.name: goal
args.description: what the survey is for, e.g. 'find the network called Office_WiFi' or 'general overview'

commands.returns: an interpreted survey of the environment, with the captured lists behind it

commands.name: agent.audit_files
commands.description: Delegates to the audit subagent the searching of the project's own files on disk - the Flipper apps that have been generated and saved with build_flipper_app: their editable C source, FAP manifest, build logs and build/edit history. Use this whenever answering the user means looking through those files, or locating one, rather than reading the device. Trigger words that should route here: search, find, look for, which app, what apps, do I have, is there an app, where is, location of, path to, the file for, the source of, the code for, the name of, list my apps, what have I built - and any question that names an app or script and asks you to locate, identify or inspect it rather than build or run it. Examples of the shape (not exhaustive): 'give me the name of the <something> app', 'find the app that failed to compile and why', 'where is the <something> app', 'what's the path to my <something> script', 'which of my apps uses the OK button?', 'do any of my apps draw to the screen?', 'what have I built so far?'. For a 'where is it located' question, answer with the app id and the file path the search returns. The audit subagent has file-search skills and NO device tools, so it can never touch the radio; it reports what it found in the files, with the app ids, file paths and lines each finding rests on. Do not guess what a generated app contains, is called, or where it lives - delegate here and answer from what the search actually returned. This searches the apps generated on this computer, not arbitrary files on the Flipper's SD card.
commands.task: Search the generated Flipper apps on disk and answer the question asked. If you do not already know which app is meant, list the apps first, then search. Report only what the file search returned - which app, which file, which line - and say plainly if nothing matched. Do not invent the contents of an app you did not search.

args.name: question
args.description: what should be found in the generated-app files, e.g. 'which app uses the OK button' or 'which build failed and why'

args.name: appid
args.description: restrict the search to one app by its id, e.g. 'paint'; omit to search every generated app

commands.returns: an answer drawn from the generated-app files, citing the app ids and files behind it

commands.name: agent.explain_subghz_capture
commands.description: Translates the raw result of a Sub-GHz capture into natural language: what type of device is likely the source of the signal (gate/car remote, sensor, weather station, etc.), based on the frequency, the detected protocol, and a purpose-built database of frequency-protocol-device correspondences, rather than just displaying the raw code as the stock Flipper application does.

args.name: frequency
args.description: the frequency to probe, in Hz

commands.returns: a natural-language explanation + the confidence level of the identification

commands.name: agent.nfc_session_summary
commands.description: Runs nfc.watch for the specified duration and builds a natural-language summary of the session: how many distinct cards/tags were seen, which one repeated, and a guess about the usage context (e.g. 'it looks like the phone interacted 3 times with the same reader, possibly a transit pass'). This answers exactly the project's initial idea: to show what a phone's NFC connected with.

args.name: duration_ms
args.description: the duration of the monitoring session

commands.returns: a text summary + a structured list of the events

commands.name: agent.identify_ir_device
commands.description: Captures an unknown IR signal and tries to deduce what type of appliance/brand emitted it, based on the timing fingerprint of the protocol (NEC, RC5, Samsung, etc.), also offering an explanation of the reasoning, not just the protocol label.
commands.returns: a guess about the type/brand of the appliance + the decoded protocol

commands.name: agent.ir_control
commands.description: Controls an IR appliance (TV, projector, audio system, air conditioner) from a request in natural language: 'turn off my tv', 'turn off this projector', 'volume up', 'next channel', 'mute the soundbar'. Works out from the request what kind of appliance it is and which function is wanted, selects only the codes that have a real chance of working, and transmits them one by one until the user presses the middle (OK) button on the Flipper to signal that the appliance reacted. Filtering by brand is the point: a Samsung TV is only ever sent Samsung codes, never other brands'. If the brand given is not in the database, the closest known name is used and the substitution is reported. If no brand is given, every brand of that appliance type is tried, which is when it behaves like a classic bruteforce. The Flipper's screen shows 'Bruteforcing IR' with a progress bar for the duration of the run. Codes come from a small built-in table first; after five unsuccessful attempts on the same appliance and button it searches an online database of thousands of real remotes automatically. Set search_online to do that immediately, which is what to do when the user says it did not work.

args.name: request
args.description: the user's request, in their own words, e.g. 'turn off my samsung tv'

args.name: brand
args.description: the appliance brand, if the user mentioned or implied one, e.g. samsung, lg, sony, epson

args.name: device_type
args.description: tv, projector, audio or ac; pass it explicitly on follow-up requests ('volume down') where the appliance is known from earlier in the conversation but not named again

args.name: function
args.description: power, volume_up, volume_down, mute, channel_up, channel_down or input; inferred from the request when omitted

args.name: search_online
args.description: search the online IR database (IRDB) for this attempt instead of the built-in codes. Set it when the user reports that a previous attempt did not work, or asks for more codes to be tried. Requires a brand: the database is far too large to search without one. Slower than the built-in table, since the codes are fetched over the network.

commands.returns: which codes were selected and why, where they came from (built-in table or the online database), how many were sent, and whether the user confirmed that the appliance responded

commands.name: agent.build_flipper_app
commands.description: Builds an actual native Flipper Zero application (a .fap) from a request in natural language: 'build me a simple paint app', 'make a stopwatch', 'a dice roller'. This does not answer with talk: it runs a three-way design debate - a proposer that researches the task on the web and writes the C source against the Flipper SDK, a challenger that argues against that design with concrete objections, and an arbiter that keeps only what survives the argument - then compiles the result with the Flipper toolchain (ufbt) and, if a device is connected, installs it. Compiler errors are fed back into the debate to be fixed, up to a bounded number of attempts. The whole debate is shown in the reasoning chain. The generated source is saved and stays editable afterwards through edit_flipper_app. This is expensive - it takes a while and costs several model requests - so warn the user before starting. The result reports the REAL compiler outcome (exit code and captured output): if the build failed it says so and relays the error; it never claims an app was built, installed or is running unless the toolchain confirmed it. Without a physical Flipper the app is still compiled for real, but installation is reported as simulated.

args.name: request
args.description: the app the user wants, in their own words, e.g. 'a simple paint app you draw on with the arrow keys'

args.name: app_name
args.description: a short human name for the app, e.g. 'Paint'; if omitted a name is derived from the request. The app id (used on disk and on the device) is derived from this by lowercasing and replacing spaces with underscores.

commands.returns: the debate's conclusion, the real compiler result (built or the error), whether it was installed or that installation was simulated, and the app id under which the source was saved for later editing

commands.name: agent.edit_flipper_app
commands.description: Changes an app that was already built with build_flipper_app: 'add a bigger brush to the paint app', 'make the stopwatch count down instead'. It locates the saved source of that app, runs the same three-way debate over the existing code with the change requested, recompiles and reinstalls. Use this rather than build_flipper_app whenever the user refers to an app that already exists - it preserves the existing app and its history instead of starting a new one. Reports the real compiler result exactly like build_flipper_app, and never claims the change worked unless the toolchain confirmed it.

args.name: app_name
args.description: the name or id of the existing app to change, e.g. 'Paint' or 'paint'

args.name: change_request
args.description: the change the user wants, in their own words, e.g. 'add a thicker brush toggled with the OK button'

commands.returns: the debate's conclusion, the real compiler result of the changed app, whether it was reinstalled or that installation was simulated, and the app id

commands.name: agent.remember
commands.description: Saves one durable fact to your persistent memory, so you still know it in future sessions after this conversation ends. Use it for things the user would expect you to remember across time: the devices they own and their brands ('the user's TV is a Samsung'), a stated preference, or a lasting, notable finding ('433.92 MHz is active at this location'). Do NOT store secrets, passwords, one-off values, or anything the user asked to keep private. Keep each fact to one short, self-contained sentence. The facts you already remember are listed in your system instruction, so check there before saving a duplicate.

args.name: fact
args.description: one short sentence to remember, e.g. 'the user's TV is a Samsung'

commands.returns: confirmation that the fact was stored, or that it was already remembered

commands.name: agent.confirm_authorized_action
commands.description: A mandatory safety gate before any device command that transmits/acts upon the real world (subghz.replay and its agent wrapper agent.replay_subghz, nfc.emulate, ir.send, and every offensive Wi-Fi/BLE command: wifi.attack_*, wifi.evil_portal, wifi.karma, ble.spam_*): the agent explicitly asks the user to confirm that they own the target or are authorized to test it, before sending the command. It executes nothing by itself, it only validates the intent.

args.name: action
args.description: the name of the device command about to be sent

commands.returns: confirmation or refusal, with the reason
